material.text: model-compare-opencode-plugin: OpenCode plugin that switches OpenRouter model aliases to the best value-for-money pick from canonical/model-compare's ranking (balanced, price, quality).

# model-compare-opencode-plugin An [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai) v2 plugin that picks the best value-for-money OpenRouter model from [canonical/model-compare](https://github.com/canonical/model-compare)'s ranking, for three priorities: `balanced`, `price`, `quality`. Ranking data comes from a vendored copy of upstream's `model_compare.py` (default) or the published `catalog.json`. Each priority is a live alias inside the existing OpenRouter provider — no new provider, no new credentials: | Alias | Resolves to | |---|---| | `openrouter/model-compare/balanced` | best all-round value pick | | `openrouter/model-compare/price` | best price pick | | `openrouter/model-compare/quality` | best quality pick | The alias re-points at the current pick while OpenCode runs (refresh every 30 minutes, data cache 6 hours). It also pins the catalog's scored reasoning effort on each request, so the model runs at the depth its `quality` score was measured at. OpenCode's model picker shows it as `Model Compare: → `, with `(fallback)` while the fallback is serving and `(unavailable)` when the alias is disabled. The alias name deliberately carries no catalog effort or alternative: OpenCode shows the selected variant itself, and a baked-in depth would not follow your `#variant` choice. **Effort vs variant.** The model-compare catalog and the request body call this reasoning level the *effort* (`quality_effort`, pinned as `reasoning.effort`); OpenCode calls the selectable model option a *variant* (`provider/model#variant`). The alias byline shows only the pick; the report dialog's status line uses “variant” and shows the highlighted model's variant. ## Install Add a `plugins` entry to `opencode.jsonc` (project or global): ```json { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "plugins": [ { "package": "model-compare-opencode-plugin", "options": { "source": "auto", "defaultPriority": "balanced", "fallback": "openrouter/z-ai/glm-5.3-flash" } } ] } ``` All options are optional — see [Configuration](#configuration). The package is on npm; OpenCode resolves and loads it itself. The terminal-UI half ships precompiled (`dist/tui.js`): OpenCode compiles plugin JSX itself only for local sources — files under a `node_modules` directory skip its Solid JSX transform and would fall back to a React compile that cannot resolve — so the published package must not ship raw JSX. To run a checkout of this repo instead, see [Development](#development). ## Usage Point sessions at an alias — as the root default in `opencode.jsonc`: ```json { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "model": "openrouter/model-compare/balanced" } ``` Per agent (in the `.md` frontmatter): ```md --- description: Reviews changes for correctness mode: subagent model: openrouter/model-compare/quality --- ``` Or via `--model`: ``` opencode run --model "openrouter/model-compare/price" "msg" ``` **Where the alias binds.** An agent's `model` applies to subagent launches everywhere, and to primary agents only when you select the agent in the TUI. Headless runs (`opencode run --agent …`) and server-side agent switches do **not** apply it — the root default (or `--model`, or `/use-best`) governs. Commands: - `/use-best [priority]` — switch the session to `openrouter/model-compare/

` (defaults to `defaultPriority`). Refuses a disabled alias. - `/model-compare` — top 5 per priority with scores and data age; each line also shows the reasoning effort behind `quality` (`· high`) and the best selectable measured alternative (`· alt max 56.0`). Priorities whose `weights` override actually takes effect are labelled `(custom weights)` with recomputed scores, and each alias's current pick is marked `← current pick`. The output is a synthetic message (`resume: false`): it costs no model turn and, in a headless session, surfaces in the transcript at the next turn. In the TUI it opens the report dialog instead, with model, quality and price columns and a status line that follows the cursor and shows the highlighted model's variant. ### Keyboard shortcuts | Key | Action | |---|---| | `alt+m` | picks dialog — all three priorities with their current picks | | `alt+u` | switch the session to the default priority's pick (the `/use-best` default); on the opening screen it creates a session bound to it | | `alt+e` | toast the last response's served endpoint, alias responses only (`!` prefix flags a downgrade — not in the steering order) | | `alt+shift+m` | report dialog — the top-5 table with a cursor-following variant status line; `return` switches the session to the highlighted model at the variant its status line advertises (`#max`, …), falling back to the bare model when the host's own registry does not offer that variant | | `return` | select the highlighted row (picks dialog: switch to that priority) | | `esc` | close the dialog | Both dialogs open anywhere — including the opening screen, where no session exists yet. There, picking a row (a priority in the picks dialog, a model in the report) creates a new session already bound to that model and opens it; merely opening a dialog never creates a session. With a session open, a pick switches that session as before. Status: the footer shows `MC: balanced → ` (balanced only — `disabled`/`unavailable`/`(fallback)` as applicable; all three priorities live in the picks dialog). The picker's alias name carries only the pick (plus the fallback marker); the report dialog's status line carries the variant. The footer stays a compact served-model line. Toasts announce `/use-best` outcomes and pick changes (never for the first observation after load), the `alt+e` served endpoint, and the cannot-steer notice — see [Steering and served endpoints](#steering-and-served-endpoints). Headless, command feedback is synthetic transcript messages at the next turn; the steering toasts have no headless surface. ## Configuration Options live under `plugins[].options`: | Option | Default | Meaning | |---|---|---| | `source` | `auto` | `auto`, `local`, or `remote`. `auto` uses the vendored script when `python3` 3.10+ is available, otherwise the remote catalog | | `defaultPriority` | `balanced` | Priority used by `/use-best` with no argument | | `fallback` | unset | `openrouter/` used when no pick is available. Only OpenRouter models work: the alias's `modelID` lives inside the `openrouter` provider. Runnability is checked at each resolution | | `weights` | upstream | Partial overrides per named priority (`quality`, `price`, `context`, `age`), merged with upstream's weights and renormalized to sum 1 | | `pinDays` | `14` | Age in days after which a pick is re-evaluated | | `minLead` | `0.03` | Score lead needed to replace a pinned pick | | `catalogURL` | published catalog | Remote source URL. The catalog is published at `https://model-compare.dev/catalog.json` — the plugin's built-in default, fetched directly over https. (The old `https://canonical.github.io/model-compare/catalog.json` home redirects to a plaintext `http://` target; the plugin fails closed on any redirect that leaves https.) Only point it at a source you trust: it decides which models can be picked | | `scriptPath` | vendored copy | Development override for a local `model_compare.py` | A present-but-invalid value logs a warning and applies the default (`weights` drop invalid entries individually; the valid remainder applies). Absent options apply defaults silently. Setup never throws; the aliases stay functional. ## Pinning and fallback Per priority the plugin keeps one pin/last-known-good record in plugin storage, keyed by the effective weights so different weight configurations don't collide. With a fresh catalog: - No pin: adopt the best candidate. - Pinned model gone or not runnable: switch to the best candidate now. - Pin older than `pinDays`: re-evaluate (which may re-adopt the same model; `since` resets on every adoption). - Otherwise: switch only when the best candidate leads the pinned pick by at least `minLead` (upstream's 0–1 score scale). Resolution order: pin (if runnable) → best runnable candidate → `fallback` (if runnable) → the alias is disabled. The fallback is never stored as a pin. Pins are advisory: concurrent OpenCode processes refresh independently, last writer wins. ## Steering and served endpoints Requests made through one of the three aliases carry the resolved pick's routing: the catalog's per-model `steering` block is injected into the request body under OpenRouter's `provider` key, so the call is routed onto the endpoints whose pricing the ranking actually ranked — not onto whatever OpenRouter's default routing picks, which can be a sub-default-quantization endpoint at a price the ranking never saw. The block comes from the catalog, whichever source produced it: the vendored script derives it from the same per-model endpoint data its pricing uses, and the published catalog carries it ready-made. Only the block's `provider` sub-object is injected — its top-level `model` field never reaches the body — and the routing object is built field by field: - `order` — the endpoints the ranking priced, cheapest blended price first; eligible endpoints whose price can't be computed are appended last rather than dropped. - `ignore` — the live endpoints the ranking excluded, so OpenRouter cannot route onto pricing it never ranked (sub-default quantizations, schedule-gate failures, variants). - `quantizations` — the precision floor: the model's default precision and anything more precise among its live endpoints. The key is omitted entirely when the model has no default precision — never sent as an empty list, which would exclude every endpoint. - `allow_fallbacks` — always `true`: when nothing in `order` can serve, OpenRouter may still route outside the list. The rules, and the exceptions: - **Aliases only.** Steering fires only when the session's model is one of the three aliases and the request's model is that alias's current pick. What decides is the request's model reference: alias references steer, concrete references never do — a model you picked directly is untouched even when it is the exact model an alias currently resolves to. Primary turns and compaction alike are steered; auxiliary calls that run a different model (title generation) are not. - **A pre-existing `provider` key wins.** If the request body already carries a `provider` key — routing you or a provider integration configured — the plugin does not inject; it never clobbers routing it did not choose. - **No steering data, no injection.** When the plugin has no catalog source, or the current pick's catalog entry carries no `steering` block, the request proceeds untouched: OpenRouter's default routing applies and the run completes normally — unsteered, not failed. With no catalog source at all, the TUI says so once per session, on the first alias request that has a pick to steer: `cannot steer this session; OpenRouter default routing applies` (skipped when that request already carries its own `provider` — then default routing is not what applies). Headless runs render no toasts; the routing behavior is identical. A disabled alias steers nothing and toasts nothing; what serves then is the binding's own fallback behavior (see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)). - **Always-on.** No option turns steering off. It is what makes the plugin's value promise — the ranked price is what you pay — true. `order` is a preference list, not a pinned destination: OpenRouter works down the list and serves from whichever ranked endpoint can take the call — which one serves is OpenRouter's decision, and with fallbacks allowed it can even land outside the list. **Which endpoint served a call.** Three ways to check: - The `alt+e` toast (see [Keyboard shortcuts](#keyboard-shortcuts)) — the current session's last primary alias response's served endpoint: `last response served by `, or `! served by — not in steering order` when the served provider matched no entry of the steering order actually applied. The report dialog's footer carries the same capture as `last response: @ `, under the note `routing steered to endpoints (aliases only)`. - The response body — every OpenRouter response names its serving endpoint in the `provider` field. - OpenRouter's dashboard — per-request endpoint records. The alt+e capture is best-effort by design, and alias-scoped: only a session whose model is one of the three aliases has responses peeked and recorded — a direct pick's or another agent's response is never read, let alone modified. The plugin peeks at only the first 4 KB of the response body — a pass-through read; the body itself flows byte-for-byte. Streaming responses carry `provider` in the first chunk, so the peek normally catches them; a non-streaming response whose `provider` field sits beyond the peek window is forwarded uncaptured, and `alt+e` then toasts nothing. The response body's `provider` field and OpenRouter's dashboard remain the authoritative verification paths. ### Reasoning depths The catalog's `reasoning.depths` records are the measured reasoning efforts behind a model's `quality` score: each row carries the effort (`max`, `high`, …), the AA intelligence index measured at that effort, and the AA `$/task` cost. `quality` is the index at `quality_effort` — the depth the ranking scored — and the plugin pins that effort on alias requests that do not already set a reasoning field or an explicit `#variant` (`reasoning: { effort }`), so the alias runs at the depth its score represents. The depths are advisory metadata, not ranking input: they explain the score and the alternative, they do not change the pick. The `/model-compare` line's `alt` label shows the best **selectable** measured alternative: the highest-index selectable effort that scores strictly higher than the scored depth (`alt max 56.0`). It is empty when the scored depth is already the best measured selectable depth — the normal case for the plugin's own sources (the vendored `--catalog` run and the published remote). A user-pointed `catalogURL` can serve an explicit-effort document where a deeper row scores higher; the label then names it. Only efforts OpenRouter can actually select are advertised: an effort must appear in the model's expanded `supported_efforts`, or be the single-state `#none` toggle. An AA row for an unlisted effort is display-only and never becomes an `alt`. The catalog's `reasoning` sentinel is a producer label for a single-state reasoning model, not a gateway value, and is never sent. An explicit `#variant` selection, or a body that already sets `reasoning`/`reasoning_effort`, wins and is never overwritten. ## Data sources - `auto` — vendored `vendor/model_compare.py` run with `python3` (no shell, 60 s timeout, minimal environment); degrades to remote when python3 is missing or the run fails. - `local` — the vendored script only; failures are reported and the pin/last-known-good pick is kept. - `remote` — HTTPS fetch of `catalogURL` with a 6-hour cache (upstream republishes every 6 hours). The last validated catalog is persisted, so ranking and `/model-compare` work offline after a restart. The cache is keyed by source (URL or script path), so changing the source never serves the previous source's data. The persisted record also carries a catalog-era version: upgrading to 0.6.2 (doc-cache records moved to v2 for the schema-v6 era) discards the cached catalog, so the first launch after the upgrade re-acquires and the aliases run on the configured fallback until that first refresh succeeds. Script exit code 2 means "no candidates" *or* an argparse usage error — never read it as "no candidates" alone. **Vendored pin:** `vendor/model_compare.py` is byte-identical to upstream `v0.7.0` (`vendor/UPSTREAM.json` records repo, tag, commit, sha256). The catalog is schema v6 (since upstream 0.7.0): `quality` is the AA intelligence index at the model's best measured selectable reasoning effort (the highest AA index at an effort OpenRouter supports, ties to the deeper effort), and every entry carries `quality_effort` plus a `reasoning` block (`default_effort`, the expanded `supported_efforts`, the raw flags, and the measured `depths` with AA `$/task` — see [Reasoning depths](#reasoning-depths)). The plugin accepts schema v6 ONLY — `validateCatalog` rejects anything else — and releases are gated on the live remote serving v6 (the release-gate check pipes `https://model-compare.dev/catalog.json` through `scripts/canary-check.mjs`, which fails closed when the served document is not the expected schema). Each alias request pins exactly the pick's `quality_effort` in its body (`reasoning: { effort }`), so the alias runs at the depth its score represents — which since 0.7.0 may be a deeper effort than the model's OpenRouter default (`quality_effort` is the scored depth, not `default_effort`); an explicit `#variant` selection, or a body that already sets `reasoning`/`reasoning_effort`, wins and is never overwritten. The catalog's `reasoning` sentinel is display-only and never sent to the gateway. Effective-tier pricing semantics still apply: `pricing` scalars hold effective-tier values — the tier in effect at 1M-token prompts — so models with OpenRouter price overrides are ranked at what a long session actually pays. **Vendored 0.7.0 cold-cache network profile:** since 0.4.0 the vendored script performs per-model endpoint-pricing fetches when building a fresh catalog (78 candidates in the recorded run). Each fetch fails closed per model — after the script's internal retries, a failed endpoint fetch drops that model and the catalog shrinks silently (429-class responses raise without retry) — so a degraded network costs pool coverage, not pricing correctness. Unkeyed runs hydrate quality from the published catalog (one fetch of `https://model-compare.dev/catalog.json`, cached under `published-catalog`; keyed runs consult the AA API — the primary quality source — and never fetch the published catalog); every quality hydration fails closed to "no quality data" per model, and a missing record at the selected effort shows `-` rather than borrowing another effort's score. A cold cache under a slow network can exceed the plugin's 60-second local budget, in which case the plugin warns and falls back (`auto` → remote, `local` → its cached document). **Upgrading the pin** — reviewed PRs only; nothing merges automatically: 1. `node scripts/sync-vendor.mjs ` — fetches the script at that commit, reports the sha256 change, re-pins `UPSTREAM.json`, prints the matching CHANGELOG section (`--check` verifies offline). 2. Conformance tests check `--version`, schema v6, required fields, recomputed `overall` scores, and the standard-library-only import allowlist. 3. The upgrade PR body lists script lines touching imports, URLs, environment variables, subprocess calls and file writes, for reviewer attention. 4. Release with a changelog line naming the upstream tag; users run `opencode plugin update` (OpenCode checks but doesn't apply). A scheduled workflow opens a draft upgrade PR when upstream publishes a newer release (never a downgrade); a nightly canary exercises the vendored script against live upstream data and asserts the generated catalog is schema v6 (`scripts/canary-check.mjs` pins `EXPECTED_SCHEMA_VERSION = 6` and exits nonzero on any other version); releases additionally gate on the live remote itself (see the publishing gates below); a weekly drift check compares the vendored sha256 against upstream's pinned commit and the published rankings against the published scores. ## Troubleshooting - **`model-compare: no ranking data for openrouter/model-compare/

`** — an agent whose `model` is that alias made a primary request while the alias was disabled. The guard aborts the request — even when the root-governed effective model is healthy — to protect the configuration's intent. Set `options.fallback` or fix the data source. Primary requests only; title/compaction/generation are untouched. - **Primary run answered with a model I didn't configure** — the root default (and `/use-best`-switched sessions) fall back silently to OpenCode's choice when the alias is disabled. Agent `model` doesn't apply on headless primary runs anyway — see the binding note above. - **Where are the plugin's warnings?** Nowhere, currently: `opencode serve` prints nothing to stdio and plugin `console.warn` reaches no log. The visible diagnosis surface is `/model-compare` — its data-age and no-data lines. - **A pick change takes a minute or two to land, and runs started meanwhile wait.** When a pick changes (at most once per 30-minute refresh), the plugin replays OpenCode's provider/model/agent registries; the harness measured ~90–105 s, with runs started during the replay blocking. Nothing is wrong. - **`Model unavailable: openrouter/model-compare/

`** — a subagent configured with a disabled alias; OpenCode fails the launch before any request, so the guard is not involved. - **Data age in `/model-compare`** — the plugin's own acquisition time of the document, not upstream's `generated_at` (set at build time even when serving inputs from cache). - **No aliases at all** — the aliases live inside the `openrouter` provider; if it is not connected in the project, they cannot be created. The plugin warns at setup and on every refresh; primary runs fall back silently. - **`Cannot find package 'react'` for `src/tui.tsx` in the CLI log** — an OpenCode install of a release that still shipped the TUI half as raw TSX: OpenCode's Solid JSX transform skips `node_modules` paths, so the installed TSX fell to a React compile. Update the plugin to a release that ships the precompiled `dist/tui.js` entry (the server half is unaffected either way). If the warning persists after updating, restart the TUI so the new package generation is picked up. ## Development Run a checkout instead of the npm package: ```json { "plugins": [ { "package": "./src", "options": { "source": "auto" } } ] } ``` OpenCode's local loader resolves a directory target strictly as `

/index.*` — `exports` are ignored for local paths, and file targets are rejected. `src/` has the physical entry files (`src/index.ts`, `src/tui.tsx`); the plugin's imports resolve from the repo's `node_modules` (`npm ci` once at the repo root). The repo ships this setup as [`.test/`](.test/README.md). Two caveats: the watcher only watches package-style entries, so source edits need an OpenCode restart; and a bare package name is always npm-installed by OpenCode — it is not read from `node_modules` — so local testing must use the directory form. ```sh npm run dev # launch the TUI against this checkout npm test # unit + vendored-conformance suites (hermetic) npm run build # regenerate dist/tui.js from src/tui.tsx MC_INTEGRATION=1 npx vitest run tests/integration/ # live-server suite (opt-in) ``` - `npm run dev` writes a scratch project under `/tmp/opencode/model-compare-dev`, points its plugin entry at this checkout's `src/`, hides the global OpenCode config for the run (so an installed `model-compare-opencode-plugin` cannot shadow the local copy), and runs `opencode --standalone` there. The isolation is config-only: the scratch project shares your OpenCode data directory (auth, plugin state, sessions), so alias switches made in the dev session rewrite your live aliases. Pass extra flags after `--` (for example `npm run dev -- --auto`), or use `--print-config` to inspect the generated project config. `MC_DEV_DIR` overrides the scratch location. Source edits need an OpenCode restart. - Local development loads `src/` directly and needs no build; the *published* package does — OpenCode's Solid JSX transform skips `node_modules` paths, so the npm-installed raw TSX cannot load (see [Install](#install) and the troubleshooting entry). `npm run build` precompiles `src/tui.tsx` through the same Babel pipeline as the host's loader (taken from the pinned `@opentui/solid`) into `dist/tui.js`, rebasing relative imports from `src/`-relative to `dist/`-relative; `prepublishOnly` runs it, and CI builds before the packaging check. `dist/` is regenerated, never committed. - The integration files skip unless `MC_INTEGRATION=1`, so plain `npm test` stays hermetic. The suite drives a real `opencode serve` on 127.0.0.1:14721 and needs the `opencode` CLI and `python3` (skips cleanly when either is missing); one case needs network access and the `sqlite3` CLI. - `node scripts/pack-smoke.mjs` (also in CI, after `node scripts/build-tui.mjs`) packs the plugin and checks the tarball against the packaging list (files, `exports`, relative imports, and that the TUI artifact is precompiled — no react import). It does **not** load the package in OpenCode — install the tarball into a scratch project and confirm OpenCode loads it before publishing. - Publishing: cut a GitHub release tagged `vX.Y.Z` and `.github/workflows/release.yaml` stages the package on npm through trusted publishing (tokenless OIDC — no token secret; the npmjs.com trusted-publisher entry must name `release.yaml`, the `canonical/model-compare-opencode-plugin` repository and the `release` environment, with "Allow npm publish" and "Allow npm dist-tag" unchecked — stage-only, npm's recommended posture). Nothing goes live until a maintainer approves it with 2FA on npmjs.com (package page → Staged Packages) or via `npm stage approve`. The workflow fails closed when the tag does not match `package.json`'s version, and the gates (build, typecheck, tests, pack-smoke, live-remote canary) run before staging. - `fixtures/catalog-v0.7.0.json` is the sole contract fixture — a recorded schema-v6 catalog; `fixtures/catalog-no-quality.json` is derived from it by `scripts/make-no-quality-fixture.py` (the vendored script's own quality-blind weights, so its scores are internally consistent). No pre-v6 fixture exists; the v6-only gate rejects one. `node scripts/sync-vendor.mjs --check` verifies the pin's sha256 offline. - Repo layout: `src/core/` (pure ranking/pinning), `src/sources/` (local + remote acquisition), `src/opencode/` (aliases, guard, commands, storage, refresh), `dist/` (generated `tui.js` artifact, gitignored), `vendor/` (pinned upstream script), `tests/{unit,conformance,integration}`. ## License GPL-3.0 — see [LICENSE](LICENSE). The vendored `vendor/model_compare.py` comes from [canonical/model-compare](https://github.com/canonical/model-compare) (GPL-3.0).
